newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Nervous Asia coffee trade sees London robusta down.
newsitem.headline: Nervous Asia coffee trade sees London robusta down.

text.p: London robusta futures prices are seen dipping later on Tuesday, but Asian dealers said they were concerned the emergence of any fresh bullish news could quickly reignite the coffee market's recent meteoric rally.
"It's (London) due US$10 lower on the numbers, but anything can happen," a dealer for a European trading house told Reuters.

"London should be slightly down, but it's very hard to call. Any kind of news might push the market (up) again," another dealer added. "The market looks like its running out of steam. We might see a correction soon."
The coffee markets in London and New York have staged an explosive rally over the past few weeks as tight supplies pushed prices to 20-year highs.
The July futures contract in London closed $45 up on the day on Monday at $2,100 a tonne after hitting a peak of $2,190.

Asian dealers said the market will probably shrug off overnight news from London that the 14-member Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) will not dismantle an export quota scheme and will seek to make it more flexible.
"With prices this high, who is going to take notice of these quotas," one dealer said. "The only thing the trade is worried about would be if the roasters push up prices and turn off consumers."
Origin selling from Asia's biggest coffee producer in Indonesia has accelerated over the past two weeks as coffee prices have soared.
"The Indonesian beans are coming out but the flow is not as strong as we thought it would be," one dealer said, adding some traders were going straight to farms to buy beans directly.
Traders said the flow of Indonesian coffee may have weakened due to the very aggressive selling pace from the country in April and a drop in output estimated at about 20 percent this year.
"Indonesia has dried up. They were very aggressive sellers last month," a trader said. "Many of the exporters are scrambling for cover."
The price of Indonesia's benchmark Grade 4 coffee, 80 defects, was seen by the trade at around $1,800-$1,850 a tonne FOB Lampung, up sharply from last week's quote of $1,545-$1,600.
The sharp rise in prices has also triggered strong selling from Vietnam, which is at the tailend of its robusta crop.
"The Vietnamese are selling quite comfortably although there are some problems getting the material out of the congested port in Ho Chi Minh," a dealer said.
One dealer estimated that Vietnam recently sold about 20,000 to 25,000 tonnes of coffee as it took advantage of the surge in prices.
The price of Vietnam's key Grade 2 coffee, 8.0 percent black and broken, was seen by regional dealers at around $1,700-$1,800 a tonne FOB Saigon against $1,500-$1,550 last week.
Trading of the robusta coffee contract on the Singapore Commodity Exchange (SICOM) on Monday reached a paltry three lots of the July contract which was settled at $2,010 a tonne.
